metadata.title: Parental emotional support and adolescent well-being

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2018 survey microdata of 15-year-olds to examine parental emotional support within and across countries. The analytic sample is restricted to students with reported parental emotional support and linked PISA outcomes (reading, mathematics, science scores and subjective well-being), with additional covariates capturing family wealth, country of origin, and school urbanicity and private/public status. The abstract does not specify whether OECD/PISA sampling weights and replicate weights were applied; therefore, the weighting approach cannot be confirmed from the provided text. Because the paper reports associations rather than training ML models, analysts would typically apply PISA sampling weights (and replicate weights if variance estimation is required) to obtain population-representative estimates and correct standard errors under the complex survey design.

data.outcome_summary: The paper uses PISA 2018 microdata of 15-year-olds to study how parental emotional support varies within countries by parents’ education level and by child gender, and how these patterns differ between countries. It further examines whether parental emotional support is associated with higher PISA achievement (reading, mathematics, science) and with students’ subjective well-being, reporting that the emotional-support–achievement and emotional-support–well-being associations are positive. The abstract indicates that differences in emotional support by parental education and gender are substantial but are largely explained by other characteristics, including family wealth, country of origin, and school urbanicity and private/public status. The excerpt does not report effect sizes, model specifications, PV combination rules, or missing-data procedures, so the magnitude of associations and the robustness of uncertainty estimates cannot be evaluated from the provided text alone.
